Everyone in hi-fi knows McIntosh, Fisher, Scott and Marantz. Far fewer know Stu Hegeman, Lincoln Walsh or James Bongiorno. Marc Silver, a veteran of more than fifty years in high-end audio, profiles eleven people whose influence outran their fame, often from personal memory.

On the electronics side, Stu Hegeman championed wide bandwidth and low phase shift in his Harman Kardon Citation circuits and the omnidirectional Hegeman Labs Model 1 loudspeaker. Sidney Stockton Smith quietly designed the Marantz Model 7 preamplifier and Model 8B power amplifier. James Bongiorno’s Ampzilla, built at Great American Sound (GAS), helped rid early solid-state amplifiers of their harshness. David Hafler co-founded Acrosound and Dynaco, whose ST-70 may be the most popular tube amplifier ever made, and devised the “Hafler circuit” for extracting ambience from stereo recordings.

Among the loudspeaker thinkers, Edgar Villchur’s acoustic-suspension design at Acoustic Research brought deep bass to compact sealed boxes and, in effect, invented the bookshelf speaker. Rudy Bozak went the other way, with huge cabinets and early aluminum-cone drivers. Lincoln Walsh conceived a phase-coherent 360-degree driver that lives on at Ohm Acoustics; Bud Fried preached time-aligned, phase-correct design; Jon Dahlquist’s DQ-10 sought electrostatic transparency with dynamic punch; and Carl Marchisotto did the math behind it before founding Alon and Nola. Bert Berlant, co-founder of the tape-recorder maker Concertone, preserved much of the industry’s history as the foremost collector of Marantz equipment and archives.

Their common thread, Silver concludes, was a commitment to sound as both science and art.

Adapted into Chinese by Fanyu Meng from an article by Marc Silver.
